title: Spark DataFrames & the Catalyst Optimizer
summary: A schema is what lets Spark optimize your job before running it. Raw RDD code is a black box to the planner; a DataFrame's structure is something Catalyst can actually reason about.

slides.markdown:
[RDDs](spark-architecture) are powerful but opaque — Spark can't see inside an arbitrary Python function to know what it's actually doing. **DataFrames** fix this by adding a schema, and that schema is what lets **Catalyst**, Spark's query optimizer, rewrite your query into a faster equivalent before ever touching data.

This is the same insight relational databases have used for decades — a declarative, structured query can be optimized in ways a black-box program can't — applied to distributed data processing. Nearly all modern Spark code is DataFrame code specifically because of this gap.

A DataFrame is conceptually an RDD of rows, plus a **schema** — named, typed columns, the same mental model as a SQL table. Datasets (in Scala/Java) add compile-time type safety on top of that same idea; in PySpark, DataFrame is effectively the only structured API most code uses.

The schema isn't decoration — it's the information Spark needs to reason about your query. Knowing that column `amount` is a `double` and column `region` is a `string` lets Spark's planner make decisions an untyped RDD of arbitrary Python objects never could, because from Spark's point of view, an RDD transformation's internals are just an opaque function.

slides.sectionTitle: Why the DataFrame API can be optimized and raw RDD code can't
slides.markdown:
When you write `df.filter(df.amount > 100).select("region")`, Spark sees a *declarative description* of what you want — filter this condition, project this column — and is free to choose how to execute it: reorder operations, push the filter down to the storage layer, skip reading columns you never asked for.

When you write an RDD transformation as `rdd.map(lambda row: my_function(row))`, Spark sees only a Python function reference. It has no idea whether `my_function` filters, transforms, or does something with side effects — it can't reorder, rewrite, or peek inside it at all. The RDD API trades optimizability for flexibility; the DataFrame API trades some flexibility for a compiler-like ability to rewrite your query.

Catalyst turns your DataFrame code into an execution plan through a sequence of phases: an **unresolved logical plan** (your code, syntax-checked but not yet validated against real table schemas), a **resolved/optimized logical plan** (rule-based rewrites like predicate pushdown applied), and a **physical plan** (a concrete choice of algorithms — which join strategy, which scan method — that executors actually run).

![Catalyst optimizer stages: logical plan, optimized logical plan, physical plan](assets/catalyst-plan-stages.svg)

assets.alt: Catalyst optimizer stages: logical plan, optimized logical plan, physical plan

slides.markdown:
**Predicate pushdown** moves a filter as close to the data source as possible — if the underlying storage format (Parquet, a JDBC database) can skip whole blocks of data that don't match the filter, Catalyst rewrites the plan to filter there instead of reading everything and filtering afterward in Spark.

**Projection pushdown** (column pruning) does the same for column selection: if your query only needs 3 of a table's 80 columns, Catalyst rewrites the plan to read only those 3 columns from a columnar format like Parquet, never touching the other 77 on disk at all.

Both optimizations can cut the actual bytes read by orders of magnitude, and both are only possible because Catalyst can see the full structure of the query — a filter buried inside an opaque RDD lambda can never be pushed anywhere.

slides.sectionTitle: Off-heap memory and whole-stage code generation
slides.markdown:
Two lower-level optimizations Catalyst (via Spark's Tungsten execution engine) applies underneath the plan:

- **Off-heap memory management** stores DataFrame data in a compact binary format outside the JVM's regular garbage-collected heap, avoiding both per-object JVM overhead and GC pauses that would otherwise scale badly with billions of small row objects.
- **Whole-stage code generation** compiles a chain of operations (filter, then project, then aggregate) into a single generated Java function at runtime, instead of interpreting each operator separately with virtual-function-call overhead between every step.

Both exist for the same reason: once Catalyst has a full physical plan, it can generate tight, specialized code for that exact plan rather than running a general-purpose interpreter over generic operators.

`.explain()` prints the physical plan Catalyst chose, and reading it is how you verify an optimization actually happened rather than assuming it did:

```python
df = spark.read.parquet("s3://bucket/sales/")
result = df.filter(df.region == "US").select("customer_id", "amount")
result.explain()

# Output (abbreviated):
# == Physical Plan ==
# *(1) Project [customer_id, amount]
# +- *(1) Filter (region = 'US')
#    +- *(1) FileScan parquet [customer_id,amount,region]
#       PushedFilters: [EqualTo(region,US)]
#       ReadSchema: struct<customer_id:string,amount:double>
```

`PushedFilters` confirms the region filter was pushed into the Parquet scan itself. `ReadSchema` confirms only the three needed columns are read — column pruning happened, even though the original table might have eighty columns. Seeing `PushedFilters: []` when you expected a pushdown is the signal something (often a UDF) blocked it.

slides.sectionTitle: When you still drop down to RDDs
slides.subTitle: RDD API vs DataFrame API
slides.markdown:
| | DataFrame API | RDD API |
|---|---|---|
| Optimizable by Catalyst | Yes — schema and declarative ops are visible to the planner | No — arbitrary functions are opaque |
| Performance (typical case) | Faster by default | Requires manual tuning to match |
| Expressiveness | Structured, column/row oriented | Arbitrary objects, arbitrary logic |
| When to use | The default — almost everything | Custom partitioning schemes, algorithms that don't fit a tabular model, low-level control the DataFrame API doesn't expose |

The practical rule: start with DataFrames always, and drop to RDDs only for a specific, narrow reason you can name — never as a general habit or a comfort-zone default.

slides.sectionTitle: A UDF silently disabling the optimizer
slides.markdown:
The moment you wrap logic in a **user-defined function (UDF)**, Catalyst treats it exactly like an RDD lambda — an opaque black box it cannot see inside. A filter condition or transformation expressed as a UDF can block pushdown, column pruning, and whole-stage code generation for everything around it, even though the surrounding code is otherwise pure DataFrame API.

The frustrating part is that this failure is invisible unless you check `.explain()` — the code runs, returns correct results, and just quietly runs several times slower than the equivalent expressed in built-in DataFrame functions, because Catalyst had to treat a chunk of the plan as an unoptimizable box. Most performance regressions traced back to "someone added a UDF where a built-in function would have worked" are found exactly this way — a diff that looks harmless, a job that mysteriously gets slower.

slides.sectionTitle: The senior habit: verify, don't assume
slides.markdown:
A junior Spark developer writes DataFrame code and assumes Catalyst optimized it well, because that's the API's whole selling point. A senior developer runs `.explain()` on anything performance-sensitive and checks specifically for `PushedFilters` and the read schema, because "the DataFrame API is optimizable" is a capability, not a guarantee — a UDF, a certain kind of join, or an unusual data source can silently opt a query out of the optimizations that made DataFrames worth using in the first place.

The instinct to verify rather than trust the abstraction is what separates "knows the DataFrame API exists" from "can actually make a slow Spark job fast."

Catalyst decides *what* to do — which filters to push, which columns to prune, which join strategy to pick. The next two topics cover the mechanics of *execution* once that plan runs: what a shuffle actually costs across the network, and how the join strategies Catalyst chooses between — broadcast versus shuffle join — actually work under the hood.
